lawyer: Abdul Malek, Advocate—For the Petitioner. Aminul Huq, Attorney-General with Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, Deputy Attorney-General, MA Hafiz, Assistant Attorney-General—For the State.
parties:
Abdul Malek ----- Petitioner
Vs.
State ----- opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Karim J: This Rule, on an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, to show cause as to why the proceedings of Special Case No. 27 of 1991 pending in the 3rd Court of Additional Sessions Judge and ex-officio Special Judge, Dhaka, should not be quashed or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Briefly stated, the prosecution case, as per First Information Report dated 27-12-90 filed by an Inspector of Anti-Corruption, is that during the time the accused-petitioner, Col (retired) Alhaj Abdul Malek, held the office of the Administrator of Dhaka Municipal Corporation, i.e. from 14-9-86 to 9-10-89, he gave approval to purchase of 6,000 sodium lights on the basis of a simple quotation and without inviting any tender, 436 sodium lights on the basis of only one tender and without calling a fresh tender as per financial rules and 5, 5, 04 sodium lights without any quotation or tender for lighting the streets from Zia International Airport towards the interior of the City of Dhaka. These six thousand sodium lights were purchased from Philips Bangladesh Limited at a cost of Taka 4 crores and 68 lakh (each light at the rate of Taka 7,800.00) at the instance of the accused-petitioner by abusing his position as the Administrator of the Municipal Corporation in order to obtain for himself or for any other persons pecuniary advantage without taking prior sanction of the concerned Ministry of the Government, which is necessary for making purchase of any commodity in excess of Taka 35 lakh. This purchase having been made without any competitive tender, the price of each light was Tk. 1,975.00 more than the market price prevalent at the relevant time as a result of which the Municipal Corporation had to incur a total financial loss to the tune of Taka 1,18,50,000.00 (Taka one crore eighteen lakh and fifty thousand), which was done by the accused-petitioner by abusing his official position as the Administrator of the corporation and in utter breach of the trust reposed in him under the law as Administrator of Dhaka Municipal Corporation in order to obtain for himself or for any other person pecuniary advantage, which is an offence under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and section 409 of the Penal Code. The further allegation against the petitioner is that he created one post of an Additional Chief Engineer and two posts of Superintending Engineer without sanction of the concerned Ministry thus causing financial loss to the Municipal Corporation. After investigation, the police submitted charge-sheet against the petitioner and the case record was sent to the learned Senior Special Judge, Dhaka, who transferred the case to to the 3rd Court of Additional Sessions Judge and ex-officio Special Judge, Dhaka. The trial Court framed a charge under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and section 409 of the Penal Code to which the accused-petitioner pleaded not guilty and the prosecution has examined one witness in support of their case. Thereupon the present Rule had been obtained by the accused-petitioner. 

 3. The case of the petitioner has been set forth in his application. It is stated that purchase of the 6,000 sodium lights was made as per unanimous decision of the tender committee comprising the petitioner as the chairman and 8 other members. The purchase was made through negotiation with Philips Bangladesh Ltd., whose representatives during negotiation expressed their inability to reduce the price of the lights on the ground that the price in the International Market was 30% higher than the price of Taka 7,800.00 quoted by them. The company however, agreed to increase the guarantee period from 6 months to one year and to replace at their own costs any light damaged or broken during installation and also to supervise the installation of the lights without any charge. The deal was concluded through an agreement after a certificate was issued by Philips Bangladesh Ltd. to the effect that the price in the International market was much higher. The importation of sodium lights was prohibited in the import policy of the Government and Philips Bangladesh Limited was the only producer of sodium lights at the relevant period and no other company was producing sodium lights in Bangladesh at that time. It is the policy of the Government that when any product is produced in the country by only one company or enterprise, the product shall be purchased through negotiation without the necessity of calling any tender. Six thousand sodium lights were purchased in phases over a period of 3 years from 1987 to 1989 inasmuch as the municipal corporation had no fund to buy all these lights at a time nor could so many lights be installed all at a time. Philips Bangladesh Limited admitted that they had received full price after supplying the lights and, as such, no offence under section 409 of the Penal Code can be said to have been committed. The company having asserted that they quoted Taka 7,800.00 as the price of each light and after supplying the materials they received full payment, no offence under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 can be said to have been constituted and, as such, the prosecution against the petitioner is misconceived and malafide. It is further stated that the purchase having been made on the unanimous decision of the tender committee of which the petitioner was merely the chairman, no individual liability could be fixed on the petitioner. The last point taken by the petitioner is that one post of Additional Chief Engineer and two posts of Superintending Engineer were created in order to cope with the increased volume of works of the corporation subject to the approval of the Government and no prosecution lies against the petitioner on this score. 

 5. Mr. Abdul Malek, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that at the material time Philips Bangladesh Ltd. being the only producer of sodium lights in Bangladesh and the importation of this item being prohibited in the import policy of the Government, it was the policy of the Government that when any product was produced in the country by only one company or enterprise, the product would be purchased through negotiation and no tender was necessary. He submits that six thousand lights were purchased through negotiation and no tender was necessary. He submits that six thousand lights were purchased in phases over a period of 3 years from 1987 to 1989, because the Municipal Corporation had no fund to purchase all these lights at a time nor could so many lights be installed at a time and so there was no question of making any purchase without prior approval of the concerned Ministry of the Government simply because the price of the lights was in excess of taka thirty-five lakh. Mr. Malek further submits that the decision for purchase of 6,000 sodium lights having been unanimously taken by the tender committee in its duly held meetings, the prosecution of the petitioner alone is not tenable, is misconceived and an abuse of the process of the court and, as such , liable to be quashed . He further submits that creation of a post of Additional Chief Engineer and two posts of Superintending Engineer does not constitute any criminal offence as this was done with the approval of the Government in order to cope with the increased volume of works of the corporation. 

 6. Mr. Aminul Haq, learned Attorney-General, submits that in a proceeding under section 561A CrPC it is not open to this court to embark upon an inquiry in order to see whether the prosecution story is true or not and that the pertinent question is whether the First Information Report prima facie discloses the commission of an offence alleged by the prosecution. In this connection Mr. Huq has referred to the decision in the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury and others vs. State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 wherein his Lordship Ahsanuddin Chowdhury J has observed as follows: 

 Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court. 

 8. Mr. Aminul Huq, learned Attorney General has drawn our attention to the relevant Rules of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation (contracts) Rules, 1984. Rule 6 provides that in the case of execution of works or procurement of any materials or goods by contract, tenders shall be invited through local newspapers or by public notice in Bengali by atfixing it on the notice board of the Corporation. Under Rule 7 no contract on behalf of the Corporation involving a value of above 5,000.00 Taka (five thousand taka) shall be made unless the tenders for the same have been previously considered by the tender committee. Rule 8 provides for approval of the Government for contracts involving a value of above taka thirty-five lakh. 

 10. Mr. Abdul Malek, learned Advocate for the petitioner, by relying on the decision in the case of Abdul Quader reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 submits that the High Court Division can interfere and should quash the proceedings if the facts are so preposterous that even on the basis of the Government circulars and the resolutions of the tender committee, no offence can be said to have been constituted and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment of the innocent accused and an abuse of the process of the court. In this connection Mr. Malek has referred to Memo. No. NEC (Policy)-23/CD. 82 dated April 9, 1982, of the Cabinet Division to the effect that where goods produced in the country are sufficient to meet the country's needs, all imports of these item should be banned after careful examination of the level of country's demand. This is supported by another Memo No Rt4/ wi-‘0/9(31 8,k/ao/w9 dated 9-8-90 the Ministry of Industries to the same effect. Mr. Malek has also referred to Circular No. 4/19/82/29 (150)-Committee dated Dhaka January 12, 1983 of the Cabinet Division to show that when commodities are produced by both Public and Private Sector Enterprises, the procurement should be made by open tender as per normal procedure at competitive price and that where there is only one Public Sector agency producing the commodity, the Ministry/Division/Corporation should procure the same by direct negotiation from the manufacturer without calling for any tender. From these circulars and memoranda one cannot conclude that at the relevant time importation of sodium lights was prohibited or that Philips Bangladesh Limited was the only producer of sodium lights in the private sector or that no tender was necessary for purchasing the lights. In any view this is a matter of assessment of evidence by the trial Court and not appropriate for an inquiry by this Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 561A CrPC. 

 11. Mr. Aminul Huq, learned Attorney-General, has referred to the decisions in the case of Hasanuddin Sarker vs. State reported in 34 DLR 287 wherein MH Rahman, J (as his Lordship then was), in delivering the judgment of the Division Bench, had observed : 

 "The learned Advocate is asking us to embark upon an enquiry and to consider the materials produced by the defence and to determine the guilt or innocence of the accused. In exercise of the power under section 561A CrPC this court cannot do so and prejudge the issue without allowing the prosecution a proper opportunity to prove its case against the accused at the 

 of trial the evidence will be produced by the prosecution as well as by the defence and it will be seen whether the accused petitioner dishonestly obtained an undue pecuniary advantage either for himself or for the contractor by corrupt or illegal means or otherwise by abusing his position as a public servant. At this stage it is premature to go into the merits of the case and arrive at any conclusion on the facts in issue." 

 12. The First Information Report and the charge-sheet bring out a case of criminal misconduct with the allegation that 6,000 sodium lights were purchased at the instance of the accuse-petitioner without competitive tender and without verifying the market price and without approval of the concerned Ministry of the Government for making purchase of commodities valued more than taka thirty-five lakh by abusing his position as Administrator of the Corporation in order to obtain for himself or for any other person pecuniary advantage. At this stage the High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 561A CrPC cannot say if the prosecution story is reliable or not once on a reading of the First Information Report and the charge-sheet it is found that prima facie an offence has been disclosed of which a competent court has taken cognizance. 

 When a prima facie case appears from the First Information Report and the charge-sheet, this court would not embark upon an enquiry as to whether the allegation is reliable or not and would not stifle the proceedings before the prosecution gets an opportunity to bring evidence in support of their case. At this stage it cannot be said that the facts are so preposterous that no case can be said to stand against the petitioner and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent accused and an abuse of the process of the court. 

 13. In this connection we may refer to the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs. State reported in 43 DLR (AD ) 50 where the former President was charged for an offence under section 19A and (f) of the Arms Act, 1978, which was challenged in a proceeding under section 561A CrPC. In that case their Lordships observed as follows: 

 14. Upon scrutiny of the First Information Report and the charge-sheet in the instant case, it cannot be said that no prima facie case appears or the prosecution is barred by law or that the court has no jurisdiction to try the case. it is not a case where interference by this court is called for to secure the ends of justice or to prevent an abuse of the process of the court. In these circumstances, we find no merit in this application. Whatever observations we have made in this judgment should not be taken to prejudge the issues at the time of hearing of the case by the trial Court. 

 In the result, the Rule is discharged. The order passed by this court staying further proceedings of special case No. 27 of 1991 is vacated. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the court below at once along with the case record.
